samples.text:
The table shows how many books adults in one country read every year in 2014 and 2024 by age groups, and the pie charts show the formats they used for reading in these two years.

Overall, the oldest group read the most books in both years, and printed books was the most popular format, although audiobooks and e-books became more popular.

In the table, people aged 65 and over read the most books. They read 16 books in 2014 and 17 in 2024. The 50–64 group read 13 books in 2014 but it decreased to 12 in 2024. The 30–49 group also read less, from 11 to 9 books. However, the youngest group, 18–29, read more books in 2024, it increased from 9 to 12.

In the pie charts, printed book was 81% in 2014 but it fell to 59% in 2024. E-book increased from 15% to 23% and audiobook increased a lot from 4% to 18%, which is more than four times. So in 2024 the printed books were still the biggest part but it was smaller than before.
samples.why: Relevant overview near the start · both visuals covered accurately but with repetitive phrasing · simple linking (However, So) · limited vocabulary (increased, read more) · errors in agreement, articles, quantifiers and a comma splice.

samples.text:
The table compares the average number of books read each year by adults in four age groups in 2014 and 2024, while the pie charts show the formats in which these books were read in the same two years.

Overall, the oldest age group read the most books in both years, and printed books remained the most popular format. However, there was a clear move towards digital formats, especially audiobooks, over the decade.

People aged 65 and over read 16 books per year in 2014, and this rose slightly to 17 in 2024. The youngest adults, aged 18 to 29, showed the biggest increase, from 9 to 12 books, whereas those aged 30 to 49 read fewer books, dropping from 11 to 9. The 50–64 age group read one book less in 2024, with the figure falling from 13 to 12.

In terms of format, printed books accounted for 81% of reading in 2014, but this share decreased to 59% ten years later. E-books grew in popularity from 15% to 23%, while the most dramatic change was in audiobooks, whose share rose more than fourfold from 4% to 18%. As a result, digital formats made up over 40% of reading by 2024.
samples.why: Clear overview of age differences and the shift to digital · key features highlighted with apt comparisons · good range of linking devices · some less common vocabulary · one minor slip (less for fewer).

samples.text:
The table sets out the average number of books read annually by adults in four age groups in 2014 and 2024, and the pie charts show the formats in which people read in those two years.

Reading habits varied by age, with the over-65s the most avid readers throughout, while the youngest adults recorded the greatest gain. Although printed books remained dominant, they lost considerable ground to digital alternatives, particularly audiobooks.

Adults aged 65 and over read 16 books a year in 2014 and 17 in 2024. The most notable change occurred among 18- to 29-year-olds, whose annual total rose by a third, from 9 to 12 books, enabling them to overtake the 30–49 age group. The latter was the only group to see a significant decline, from 11 books to 9, while readers aged 50 to 64 dipped marginally from 13 to 12.

As for format, printed books accounted for 81% of reading in 2014 but only 59% a decade later. E-books increased their share from 15% to 23%, and audiobooks, which represented a mere 4% in 2014, expanded more than fourfold to 18%. Consequently, digital formats together made up over two fifths of all reading by 2024, compared with under a fifth ten years earlier.
samples.why: Well-crafted overview of both visuals · key changes selected and compared precisely (overtaking, combined digital share) · cohesion managed skilfully · precise, natural vocabulary (avid, lost ground) · error-free, varied structures.
